evidence.quote:
STR Submission Methods for Regulated Entities
Upon the launch of STREAMS 2, regulated entities will no longer be able to submit STRs via email, fax, or post. All STRs must be submitted electronically through STREAMS 2. Under STREAMS 2, regulated entities will have three submission options:-
Submit STR via XML Submission (Hong Kong Post e-cert is required);
Upload a completed STR in prescribed PDF format in STREAMS 2 (Hong Kong Post e-cert is required); and
Complete the STR web-form directly in STREAMS 2.

User Account Registration
For reporting institutions who wish to open STREAMS 2 user accounts, please complete the “STREAMS 2 User Registration Form”, available for download on JFIU website and submit the completed form to JFIU (jfiu@police.gov.hk).

The retained resubmission question therefore remains open. Assumptions for provisional timing tests: interpret the stated times as Asia/Hong_Kong (UTC+08:00), although the selection does not identify a timezone; treat the blackout as the half-open interval [T_start, T_resume), where T_start = 2026-01-28T00:00:00+08:00 and T_resume = 2026-02-02T09:00:00+08:00. These are interpretations for testing, not additional express provisions or evidence that the announced operational transition occurred. Branch 1, event time t < T_start: the quoted blackout instruction does not establish a routing or follow-up obligation for this event. Test: an urgent-information event immediately before T_start, in Asia/Hong_Kong, falls outside the blackout branch; resubmission requirement and deadline remain unknown. Branch 2, T_start <= t < T_resume and urgent information requires immediate STR submission: the notice directs approach by email, phone or fax. Test: such an event exactly at T_start, in Asia/Hong_Kong, enters this branch; subsequent resubmission and its deadline remain unknown. Branch 3, T_start <= t < T_resume without that urgency condition: the selection supplies no alternative timing or channel rule. Test: an event immediately before T_resume, in Asia/Hong_Kong, that does not require immediate submission does not satisfy the express urgent-contact trigger; no permission to delay is inferred. Branch 4, t >= T_resume: the notice announces resumed receipt in STREAMS 2, but supplies no follow-up rule for earlier alternative-channel contacts or new events. Test: an attempted STREAMS 2 submission exactly at T_resume, in Asia/Hong_Kong, falls outside the assumed blackout interval; neither actual receipt nor completion of any earlier reporting obligation follows from the scheduled reopening alone.

registered  person should not offer any gift other than a discount of 
fees or charges.

The underlying purpose of this requirement is to 
avoid the use of gifts to distract investors from the 
features and risks of a particular product.  In this 
regard, if gifts are offered in such a way that they are 
linked to a particular type of investment product such 
as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain 
fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this 
requirement as investors may be distracted from the 
unique features and risks of such particular funds.

The underlying purpose of this requirement is to avoid the use of gifts to distract investors from the features and risks of a particular product. In this regard, if gifts are offered in such a way that they are linked to a particular type of investment product such as certain types of funds or funds offered by certain fund houses, then such gifts will be bound by this requirement as investors may be distracted from the unique features and risks of such particular funds.

No supplied selection states whether components must be analyzed separately when they are independently offered, separately priced, separately selectable, or separately documented.
No supplied selection states an inseparability test or defines when a package is treated as one gift for paragraph 3.11.
No supplied selection states a dominant-character, principal-purpose, or predominant-benefit test for mixed gift packages.
No supplied selection explains how to classify a package containing both a permitted fee or charge discount and another benefit.
No supplied selection provides adjudicated facts applying paragraph 3.11 to a mixed or bundled package.
Applicability to a particular package, intermediary, client type, transaction structure, and timing remains unestablished from the supplied extracts.
next_source_questions: Does the SFC have official guidance, FAQ text, circulars, disciplinary decisions, tribunal or court decisions, or adjudicated interpretations that define component boundaries for a package containing multiple benefits offered in connection with an investment product?
Has the SFC stated a separability test based on independent selection, pricing, documentation, delivery, or contractual obligation?
Has the SFC stated an inseparability or dominant-character test, including the factors that determine the package's principal purpose or predominant benefit?

value.proposition: The supplied SFC Code and FAQ support only that gifts offered while promoting a specific investment product are restricted (with a stated exception for discounts of fees or charges) and that gifts linked to a particular product type or fund house fall within the requirement because of the risk of distracting investors from product features and risks. value.proposition: Express provision: paragraph 3.11 states that, when promoting a specific investment product to a client, a licensed or registered person should not offer any gift other than a discount of fees or charges. FAQ Q1 explains that gifts linked to particular product types or fund houses are bound by the requirement. Neither supplied passage establishes a dominant-character test, an inseparability test, or an authoritative rule for identifying components of a mixed package. Assumptions for the following analytical tests: the offeror and promotion fall within paragraph 3.11; the package contains a genuine fee or charge discount and a distinct non-discount gift; and no separately established exemption applies. These are conditional assumptions, not findings about any actual offer. Typed component decomposition: D = a reduction of an identified fee or charge; G = a benefit other than such a reduction; U = a benefit whose classification cannot be determined from its terms; R = the conditions linking the benefits, including eligibility, acceptance, redemption and cancellation. These types are analytical aids, not categories expressly adopted by the supplied authority. Separable-package test: if D and G can be accepted and supplied independently, assess each benefit against the stated exception. The textual inference is that D fits the exception and G does not; offering them together supplies no textual basis for sheltering G under D. Removing G would leave only D for assessment under paragraph 3.11, without establishing compliance with other requirements. Inseparable-package test: if receipt of D necessarily entails receipt of G, the selections provide no express rule for treating the whole package as a discount, classifying it by its dominant value or purpose, or allocating its benefits. If G remains identifiable as a non-discount gift, the textual inference is that its compulsory attachment to D does not itself bring G within the exception. That inference does not establish an authoritative component-boundary rule or the treatment of an indivisible benefit classified as U. The retained authority question therefore remains open.

reading.complex_classification.statement: [TRUE_IS_SATISFIED] The result answers whether an in-scope Fund satisfies a ground under the retained circular requiring treatment as a complex product for distribution. True means its total direct and indirect exposure to private market assets amounts to at least 50% of NAV, including exactly 50%, or an SFC case-specific complex-product designation is operative. False means both grounds are established absent at the assessment time; it does not establish non-complexity under every applicable rule. Either established ground suffices for true; otherwise unresolved evidence remains unknown. An excluded fund is outside scope, not a false classification result. Private market assets means private credit and private equity, with non-exhaustive indirect routes including BDCs, CLOs, TRSs and SRTs. Below 50%, footnote 7 confirms the SFC's holistic discretionary assessment, considering aggregate exposure, investment strategy, portfolio composition, liquidity and/or risk profile, asset extent and characteristics including CLO tranches and ratings and SRT structures and underlying assets, and home-regulator distribution conditions. These non-exhaustive factors do not mechanically designate a fund. Listed closed-ended alternative asset funds are excluded and referred to their separate circular. The separate 15% direct-investment limit neither displaces the 50% aggregate classification threshold nor authorises investments below it. Classification entails prevailing complex-product sales requirements, including investor suitability irrespective of solicitation or recommendation. Managers should select distributors with sufficient product knowledge, including knowledge of complex status. Existing-fund managers are expected to review, act, update offering documents as soon as practicable and communicate properly with distributors; early SFC consultation is encouraged where classification is doubtful. Potential exposure invokes disclosure guidance and may prompt closer scrutiny or FASTrack exclusion for new applicants, without itself establishing complex classification. Earlier uncertainties remain unresolved: the source supplies no commencement or fixed transition date, complete exposure-measurement basis, observation schedule or declassification procedure, and fund-specific classification evidence and referenced rules are missing.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.
5 For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

6 Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs). For LAFs, please refer to the circular on LAFs: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=25EC9
7 In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.

8 Paragraph 5.5 of the SFC’s Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission and Chapter 6 of the SFC’s Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms, and the relevant Frequently Asked Questions.

9 Issued by the SFC on 30 April 2014 and subsequently updated on 4 March 2016. Please refer to: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=16EC11

citations.quote: This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard.

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.
In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.
Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs).

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.

node.bcbaf48b0c00369eac79c2cb.distinction: The scope-and-definition challenge supports refining the parent, not adding a rival threshold rule. The assessed Fund, its manager, the SFC, distributors and intermediary instruments have distinct roles. A listed BDC can transmit private-market exposure without its listed or closed-ended form excluding the investing Fund; the LAF exception concerns the assessed Fund itself. A direct-only or listed-instrument exclusion hypothesis fails against the express inclusion of indirect exposure. A mandate-based rival is suggested by prospective disclosure examples but not established as a classification calculation rule. The strongest unresolved issue is how to quantify indirect exposure, especially mixed underlying pools and derivatives; adopting full position value or proportional look-through would manufacture an executable rule absent supporting authority. The supplied incomparable-binding diagnostics contain no substantive counterexample. Fact bindings therefore remain stable with the parent.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.
5 For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

6 Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs). For LAFs, please refer to the circular on LAFs: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=25EC9
7 In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.

8 Paragraph 5.5 of the SFC’s Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission and Chapter 6 of the SFC’s Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms, and the relevant Frequently Asked Questions.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.
5 For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

6 Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs). For LAFs, please refer to the circular on LAFs: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=25EC9
7 In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.

8 Paragraph 5.5 of the SFC’s Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission and Chapter 6 of the SFC’s Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms, and the relevant Frequently Asked Questions.

9 Issued by the SFC on 30 April 2014 and subsequently updated on 4 March 2016. Please refer to: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=16EC11

reading.edda_preprocessing.distinction: This answers which checks and conditional methods the source describes and which unknowns prevent deciding a particular request. It returns neither a Boolean compliance, prohibition, eligibility or licensing decision nor a scalar value. Authorisation and identification are cumulative objectives; the alternatives within each objective are illustrative methods. Ownership evidence, identity matching and bank acceptance are not individually exhaustive processing permissions. Formalization is null because the qualitative answer includes non-exhaustive reasonable measures, qualified responses and missing external requirements that cannot faithfully be represented by the permitted scalar expression fragment without substituting opaque compliance facts.
questions: What evidence supports treating the firm’s authorisation and identification measures as reasonable for this request?
What unresolved red flags or failed checks call for decline, withholding or follow-up before further processing?
What additional conditions arise from applicable bank contracts and unavailable referenced provisions?
reading.edda_preprocessing.statement:
The actual question answered is: before processing a new simplified eDDA setup request, what account-owner authorisation and identification checks should the firm perform, what alternatives are described, and what facts prevent a determinate processing decision? The proposed reading is that the firm should take reasonable steps both to ascertain that the owner authorised the setup request and to ensure that the owner’s submitted identification information is properly verified. Measures should be commensurate with the nature, scale and complexity of the firm’s business and operations. Both objectives apply; the methods introduced by 'may include' are illustrative rather than exhaustive or automatically sufficient.

The covered firms are licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities receiving client deposits. eDDA is an FPS service involving pre-authorised debits from the payer’s own-name account. In simplified setup, the firm is payee and initiates the request on the client’s pre-authorisation and information; the client is payer and intended account owner. The firm’s payee bank transmits the request to the designated account’s payer bank for verification and acceptance. The typical information includes bank name, account number, owner name, bank-opening identification-document type and corresponding number. Possession of these details or access to the trading account does not establish genuine authorisation because impersonation and unauthorised access are identified risks. Where setup proceeds without owner confirmation, the initiating firm bears primary responsibility for obtaining proper owner authorisation. Its bank may also require an authorisation assurance and indemnity; the actual contractual requirements are unknown.

For authorisation, where the payer bank requires owner confirmation during setup, the described method is to assess whether that bank has robust authentication for confirming owner authorisation. Appropriate enquiries may be made through the payee bank or directly with the payer bank. A confirmation requirement or use of a banking app or website alone does not establish robustness. Where owner confirmation is not required, or this first method cannot be satisfied, the described alternative is to ascertain ownership through a one-off small-value transfer from the designated bank account to the firm’s designated bank account for credit to the client’s trading account, and verify the account holder’s name against the transfer deposit record obtained by the firm from its own bank. Footnote 6 says firms should refrain from relying solely on client-provided deposit documents. No numerical small-value threshold is supplied. The source places this ownership method under the authorisation objective; it does not establish that ownership and genuine authorisation are interchangeable in every case.

For identification, the described first method is to accept only owner information identical to the firm’s records of the requesting client, including name, the type of identification document used to open the bank account and its corresponding number. If the information differs, the described alternative is obtaining the document purportedly used to open the bank account for verification. A mismatch therefore does not automatically compel rejection, while merely obtaining a document does not automatically establish proper verification. Neither method displaces the authorisation objective. Other reasonable measures are not excluded by 'may include', but their adequacy cannot be inferred from this packet.

Footnote 4 adds that the firm should have regard to applicable limits on the number of designated deposit and withdrawal accounts, including eDDA-linked accounts, and subject those accounts to its same bank-account registration mechanism. No numerical account limit is supplied. Footnote 5 adds a distinct initial-deposit safeguard: for clients onboarded through the 'online onboarding of clients using a designated bank account in Hong Kong' approach, firms should refrain from accepting the initial deposit through simplified eDDA unless satisfied that the owner authorised setup. This exception to the stated restraint is not an unconditional permission to accept the deposit or a waiver of the other checks.

Where either checking objective cannot reasonably be satisfied, or ongoing monitoring detects red flags indicating fraud, unauthorised access or other suspicious transactions or activities, the firm should, where appropriate, decline setup and/or withhold eDDA Deposit instructions and subsequent instructions or requests relating to the relevant account or transactions, and take follow-up action before processing further. Illustrative red flags include repeated setup or deposit failures; frequent and/or large deposits within a short period without apparent legitimate purpose or commercial rationale; deposits inconsistent with financial profile, expected activity or historical patterns; new setup and new-wallet whitelisting in either order, particularly for existing clients; and unusual or suspicious deposits converted into virtual assets followed shortly by withdrawal requests. These indicators supply no fixed numerical rejection rules. The circular recalls obligations to investigate promptly and assess further action, including reporting to the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit or the Hong Kong Police Force’s Anti-Deception Coordination Centre as appropriate. Footnote 8 preserves relevant and applicable SFC notification obligations. A red flag is not stated to require automatic reporting to every listed authority.

Surrounding controls remain relevant without all becoming express per-request prerequisites. Before entering or continuing simplified arrangements, the firm should understand bank contracts and exposures, review indemnities, identify supported payer banks and confirmation requirements, and assess risks, operational capability, mitigation and financial resources for potential claims. Assessments should be reviewed periodically and upon material changes to scale or risk profile. Firms should consider supplementary amount or frequency limits, withholding periods or step-up authentication in light of client profiles, risk assessment and relevant indicators. If risks cannot be adequately mitigated, they should use standard eDDA, bank transfers or other appropriate means. Standard setup is initiated by the client through the client’s own bank.

Firms should disclose settings, including applicable limits and expiry dates, obtain client consent and remind clients to review or amend settings with payer banks as needed. They should remind clients to review registered accounts and changes, monitor transactions and contact the firm or bank immediately upon spotting suspicious activity and/or report to the police as appropriate. Footnote 9 calls for reviewing client agreements, amending them where necessary and promptly notifying clients of related changes. SFC engagement with stakeholders does not suspend continuing risk assessment and mitigation.

No request-specific processing decision can be made from the supplied material. Unknown facts include genuine owner authorisation; the payer bank’s confirmation requirement and authentication strength; relevant enquiries and contractual assurances or indemnities; transfer provenance, destination, trading-account credit and the firm-bank record; identity matching and document-verification outcomes; account counts, applicable limits and registration; onboarding route and initial-deposit status; red flags and unresolved follow-up; and the adequacy of controls, operational capability and financial resources. Reasonableness, robustness, appropriateness and adequate mitigation require contextual judgment. Neither success nor failure on these matters is assumed.

Checking the whole packet and footnotes leaves the earlier source uncertainties unresolved. The full Code of Conduct paragraphs 4.3 and 12.5, VATP Guidelines paragraphs 11.10 and 16.7, AML/CFT Chapters 5 and 7, HKICL material and paragraph 20 of the layering circular are unavailable. Both listed missing dependencies lack supplied contents, hashes and reliable mappings to particular references. Exact internal paragraph numbering is not fully displayed. The layering circular was issued on 2025-11-17; this circular’s exact issue and effective dates are not supplied and cannot be derived from SFO/IS/033/2026. No fixed review interval, transfer deadline or withholding duration is stated. This is one proposed interpretation of the checks and unresolved dependencies, not approval or rejection of a particular request.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) issues this circular to highlight the risks associated with the increasing use of simplified Electronic Direct Debit Authorisation (eDDA)1 arrangements2 by licensed corporations, SFC-licensed virtual asset service providers and associated entities (collectively referred to as “licensed firms”), such as internet brokers and virtual asset trading platform operators, for receiving client deposits. These risks include those arising from erroneous, unauthorised or fraudulent eDDA setup requests and subsequent direct debit transactions (referred to as “eDDA Deposits”). This circular also sets out measures for assessing and mitigating such risks to assist licensed firms in protecting their operations and clients from financial losses.
Background of simplified eDDA arrangements

Licensed firms adopt simplified eDDA arrangements to enable clients to transfer funds from their own bank accounts (ie, same-name accounts) to their trading accounts through licensed firms’ mobile trading applications or trading websites, thereby facilitating a more efficient deposit process for trading or settlement purposes.
The simplified eDDA setup process adopted by a licensed firm typically involves the following steps:

(a) a client provides the licensed firm, through the firm’s mobile trading application or trading website, with pre-authorisation and necessary personal and bank account information for the firm, as payee, to initiate an eDDA setup request for withdrawing funds from the client’s designated bank account. Such information generally includes the bank’s name, bank account number, bank account owner’s name, the type of identification document used to open the bank account, and the corresponding identification document number; and

(b) the setup request, together with the information provided by the client, is then submitted to the licensed firm’s bank (ie, the payee bank), which further transmits the request and information to the bank at which the client’s designated bank account is maintained (ie, the payer bank) for verification and acceptance.

Subject to the payer bank’s practices and the commercial arrangements between the payee bank and the payer bank, the payer bank may or may not require the bank account owner (ie, the licensed firm’s client as payer) to confirm the eDDA setup request. Where confirmation is required, it is usually conducted through the payer bank’s mobile banking application or internet banking website. The setup process generally takes longer if confirmation is required.

Where confirmation from the bank account owner is not required, the licensed firm may be required by its bank to confirm that authorisation from the bank account owner has been obtained. More importantly, the licensed firm may also be required to indemnify its bank against any losses or liabilities the bank may incur, including third-party claims, arising from the processing of eDDA setup requests or subsequent eDDA Deposits.
Risks associated with simplified eDDA arrangements

When a simplified eDDA setup request is processed without confirmation from the bank account owner, the licensed firm that initiates the setup request and subsequent eDDA Deposits at the client’s request bears primary responsibility for ensuring that it has obtained proper authorisation from the bank account owner. This exposes the firm to risks, including:

(a) Impersonation and unauthorised access risks: An eDDA setup request may be initiated without the bank account owner’s knowledge, particularly in cases involving impersonation or unauthorised access to a client’s trading account, where stolen personal and bank account information is used to initiate the eDDA setup; and

(b) Indemnity and financial risks: The firm faces financial risks arising from the indemnity provided to the payee bank, including in cases of fraudulent or unauthorised eDDA setup requests or eDDA Deposits, as well as disputes or claims arising from erroneous eDDA setup requests containing inaccurate information submitted by the firm based on the information provided by its clients.
Measures for risk assessment and mitigation

Licensed firms are reminded of their obligations to maintain proper internal control procedures and adequate financial and operational capabilities to protect their operations and clients from financial loss arising from fraud and other dishonest acts3. In this regard, licensed firms adopting simplified eDDA arrangements for receiving client deposits should review these arrangements, assess the associated risks, and implement appropriate risk mitigating measures.
Risk assessment of simplified eDDA arrangements

Licensed firms are reminded to have a thorough understanding of simplified eDDA arrangements for receiving client deposits, as well as their related risk exposures and obligations. For example, they should review the relevant service agreements, terms of business and other contractual documents with their banks.
Before entering into or continuing with existing simplified eDDA arrangements, licensed firms should:
(a) review the terms of any indemnities provided, or to be provided, to their banks;

(b) identify the payer banks for which their payee banks can facilitate simplified eDDA arrangements, and understand whether such payer banks require confirmation from bank account owners for eDDA setup requests;

(c) assess the relevant risks arising from (b), including those from erroneous, unauthorised or fraudulent eDDA setup requests and eDDA Deposit instructions, as well as the firms’ operational capabilities to address such risks, having regard to the risk mitigating measures that the firms may adopt, and their financial resources to meet potential claims; and

(d) review the risk assessment in (c) periodically and whenever material changes occur to the scale or risk profile of their simplified eDDA arrangements, having regard to risk factors including those mentioned in paragraph 6.
Measures to mitigate the risks associated with simplified eDDA arrangements

Licensed firms should implement risk mitigating measures commensurate with the nature, scale and complexity of their business and operations. Specifically, before processing any new simplified eDDA setup requests from their clients4, licensed firms should:
(a) take reasonable steps to ascertain that the eDDA setup request is authorised by the bank account owner5, which may include:

(i)  where confirmation from the bank account owner is required by a payer bank during the setup process, assessing whether the payer bank has a robust authentication process for confirming that eDDA setup requests are authorised by bank account owners; to facilitate this assessment, appropriate enquiries may be made through the payee bank or directly with the payer bank; or

(ii)  where confirmation from the bank account owner is not required or where (i) cannot be satisfied, ascertaining the ownership of the bank account designated for the eDDA setup by requiring the client to make a one-off small-value fund transfer from that bank account to the licensed firm’s designated bank account for crediting to the client’s trading account, and verifying the account holder’s name against the deposit record for that transfer obtained by the licensed firm from its bank6; and
(b) take reasonable steps to ensure that the identification information of the bank account owner submitted in the eDDA setup requests is properly verified, which may include:

(i)  accepting only identification information of the bank account owner that is identical to the firm’s records of the client who makes the eDDA setup request; such information includes the name, the type of identification document used to open the bank account, and the corresponding identification document number; or

(ii)  where the identification information used for the eDDA setup request differs from that held by the firm, obtaining the identification document purportedly used to open the bank account for verification.

Where the measures in paragraph 10(a) or 10(b) cannot be reasonably satisfied, or where licensed firms detect red flags indicating fraudulent activities, unauthorised access, or other suspicious transactions or activities as part of their ongoing monitoring7, licensed firms should, where appropriate, decline the eDDA setup requests and/or withhold the processing of eDDA Deposit instructions and any subsequent instructions or requests relating to the relevant account or transactions, and take follow-up actions before processing further. Examples of red flags include:
(a) repeated failures in eDDA setup requests or deposits;
(b) frequent and/or large eDDA Deposits made by the clients within a short period without an apparent legitimate purpose or commercial rationale;
(c) eDDA Deposits that are inconsistent with a client’s financial profile, expected account activity or historical deposit patterns;
(d) a new eDDA setup request followed by the whitelisting of a new wallet address for depositing or withdrawing virtual assets, or vice versa, particularly in the case of existing clients; and
(e) unusual or suspicious eDDA Deposits that are subsequently converted into virtual assets, followed by instructions or requests to withdraw the virtual assets shortly thereafter.

Licensed firms are reminded of their obligations to promptly investigate and assess whether such transactions or activities warrant further actions including reporting to the relevant authorities, such as the Joint Financial Intelligence Unit or Anti-Deception Coordination Centre of the Hong Kong Police Force (HKPF), as appropriate8.

Licensed firms should consider implementing supplementary measures to further mitigate the risks arising from the processing of eDDA setup requests and deposits. For example, they may impose appropriate restrictions on eDDA Deposits, such as limits on transaction amounts or frequency, or a withholding period after eDDA Deposits9, or require appropriate step-up authentication for an eDDA setup request or eDDA Deposit instruction, having regard to the client’s profile and the assessment referred to in paragraph 9 above, as well as other relevant risk indicators including those mentioned in paragraph 11.

Where licensed firms are unable to adequately mitigate the risks associated with the use of simplified eDDA arrangements for receiving client deposits, they should use alternative deposit arrangements, such as standard eDDA, bank transfers or other appropriate means, having regard to the nature, scale and complexity of their business and operations.
Disclosure and reminder to clients

Licensed firms should disclose the eDDA settings (including any limits on transaction amounts or frequency and any expiry dates) to clients, obtain their consent to such settings, and remind clients to review and amend those settings with the relevant payer banks as needed.

Furthermore, to promptly identify erroneous, unauthorised or fraudulent eDDA setup requests or deposits, licensed firms should also remind clients to regularly review the bank accounts being registered with the licensed firm for eDDA Deposits, including the number of such accounts and any changes or amendments made to them, and closely monitor their bank account transactions for irregularities, and contact the firm or their banks immediately after spotting any suspicious activities, and/or report the matter to the HKPF, as appropriate.

The SFC recognises the importance of the safe and effective use of simplified eDDA arrangements for receiving client deposits, and has been engaging with relevant authorities and stakeholders about the safeguards and controls associated with these arrangements. Licensed firms should, nevertheless, continue to assess the risks associated with their use of such arrangements and implement appropriate measures to mitigate those risks.

reading.ucits_prior_approval.statement: From 2025-11-28, this circular removes prior SFC approval for a covered UCITS fund's post-authorisation material change to an investment objective, policy or restriction if the change complies with home-jurisdiction requirements, involves neither novel nor complex product features, and has no potential local policy implications, subject to the application transition. Covered funds are UCITS domiciled in France, Luxembourg, Ireland or the Netherlands, and UK-domiciled collective investment schemes authorised as UK UCITS. Novelty, complexity or possible Hong Kong policy implications each excludes relief; failure to satisfy home requirements likewise leaves the otherwise applicable approval requirement in place. Home compliance must be established under the applicable home rules, not assumed from home supervision alone. If the SFC received an application before 2025-11-28 and approval or authorisation remained outstanding at commencement, the SFC continues processing it under the existing process even if the change would otherwise qualify for relief. This does not itself establish the outcome of that process or automatically dispose of the application. Management companies remain subject to applicable notification and filing requirements, whose full content is not supplied. The SFC continues post-vetting and may make follow-up enquiries or take regulatory action for non-compliance. The particular approval outcome for an excluded or transitional case remains dependent on the existing rules and missing implementing materials.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) regularly reviews its operational processes and guidance to ensure their efficiency without compromising investor interests and protection.

The SFC has further streamlined measures for processing certain post-authorisation matters for UCITS funds1, following its review and engagement with market participants. These measures aim at facilitating UCITS funds in implementing changes that are subject to their home regulator’s supervision, and will take immediate effect.
Further streamlined measures for UCITS funds
The key streamlined measures cover the following post-authorisation matters:
(i)        Change of key operators – Removing the SFC’s requirement on prior approval for change of depository and investment delegates which are under the home regulator’s supervision.

(ii)       Material changes in investment objectives, policies and restrictions – Removing the SFC’s requirement on prior approval for material changes in investment objectives, policies and restrictions which comply with the fund’s home jurisdiction requirements, except for changes that involve novel or complex product features and/or which may have local policy implications.
(iii)      Post-authorisation notifications – To align the SFC’s notification requirements with the fund’s home jurisdiction requirements, including the notice periods and content requirements.

The SFC has updated and published on its website relevant FAQs2 , including a revamped FAQ on SFC Authorization of UCITS Funds to facilitate UCITS fund managers in navigating post-authorisation compliance matters, as well as related forms and checklists3 .
Implementation
The streamlined measures set out in the relevant FAQs will take effect on 28 November 2025 (Effective Date).

Existing applications received by the SFC before the Effective Date for which no approval or authorisation has been granted will be processed by the SFC in accordance with the existing approval or authorisation process.
Obligation of management companies

The SFC will continue to conduct post-vetting of scheme changes (including those not subject to the SFC’s prior approval) and related revised documents filed with the SFC. It may make follow-up enquiries and/or take appropriate regulatory actions in case of non-compliance to ensure investor protection.
Should you wish to clarify any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission

1 For this circular, UCITS funds means (i) Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) domiciled in France, Luxembourg, Ireland and the Netherlands, and (ii) collective investment schemes domiciled in the United Kingdom authorised as UK UCITS.
2 Please refer to https://www.sfc.hk/en/faqs/Publicly-offered-investment-products
3 Please refer to https://www.sfc.hk/en/Forms/products/Investment-products-Forms-and-checklists

Further streamlined measures for UCITS funds
The key streamlined measures cover the following post-authorisation matters:
(i)        Change of key operators – Removing the SFC’s requirement on prior approval for change of depository and investment delegates which are under the home regulator’s supervision.

(ii)       Material changes in investment objectives, policies and restrictions – Removing the SFC’s requirement on prior approval for material changes in investment objectives, policies and restrictions which comply with the fund’s home jurisdiction requirements, except for changes that involve novel or complex product features and/or which may have local policy implications.
(iii)      Post-authorisation notifications – To align the SFC’s notification requirements with the fund’s home jurisdiction requirements, including the notice periods and content requirements.

The SFC has updated and published on its website relevant FAQs2 , including a revamped FAQ on SFC Authorization of UCITS Funds to facilitate UCITS fund managers in navigating post-authorisation compliance matters, as well as related forms and checklists3 .
Implementation
The streamlined measures set out in the relevant FAQs will take effect on 28 November 2025 (Effective Date).

Existing applications received by the SFC before the Effective Date for which no approval or authorisation has been granted will be processed by the SFC in accordance with the existing approval or authorisation process.
Obligation of management companies

The SFC will continue to conduct post-vetting of scheme changes (including those not subject to the SFC’s prior approval) and related revised documents filed with the SFC. It may make follow-up enquiries and/or take appropriate regulatory actions in case of non-compliance to ensure investor protection.
Should you wish to clarify any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission

1 For this circular, UCITS funds means (i) Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) domiciled in France, Luxembourg, Ireland and the Netherlands, and (ii) collective investment schemes domiciled in the United Kingdom authorised as UK UCITS.
2 Please refer to https://www.sfc.hk/en/faqs/Publicly-offered-investment-products
3 Please refer to https://www.sfc.hk/en/Forms/products/Investment-products-Forms-and-checklists

node.1bf6918f69c6b37738daeb83.distinction: The refinement separates defined fund status, the kind of change and the regulator's selected control. A UCITS domiciled outside the enumerated jurisdictions is outside scope, rather than a failed in-scope eligibility case. A supervised operator change also does not become a material investment change merely because both receive streamlining. The tested rival would make introductory home supervision an additional item (ii) condition: it could exclude an otherwise home-compliant change lacking such supervision. That rival has some support in the introduction, but 'aim at' and the express supervision language in item (i), contrasted with item (ii)'s compliance language, do not establish a second executable condition. The strongest remaining uncertainty is whether the pending-application transition preserves substantive requirements. No comparable fact-bound counterexample was supplied; incomparability diagnostics do not establish disagreement on a shared case.

node.4d548f2e09bc36ef51212f64.distinction: The text supports a clear removal-of-approval eligibility rule for changes outside the transition, rather than rival conjunctive and disjunctive exception rules. For example, an ordinary home-compliant investment-policy change in a covered Irish UCITS after the Effective Date qualifies if it has no possible local policy implications; the same change with possible local policy implications does not qualify even if it is neither novel nor complex. For an otherwise identical application received on 27 November 2025 and pending at transition, existing processing applies and this formal control gives no answer. The strongest uncertainty is whether that preserved processing also necessarily preserves the substantive approval prerequisite.
